Each task teaches one topic through a worksheet, a question bank, and an answer key, each rendered by a slim HTML viewer. Full conventions live in the repo root **`CLAUDE.md`** — read it before starting. ## The workflow (do these in order) ### 1. Understand the topic From the discussion or the "create task on " request, pin down: - the single concept and the concrete skill the student should walk away with; - which earlier tasks it builds on (skim `docs/tasks.html` for the sequence); - whether it is **C-code + debugger** based, **shell** based, or a **tools/reference** task (some tasks — e.g. task12 images, task13 command checklist — are not the full six-file shape); - any **staged vocabulary** the user is deliberately withholding (e.g. the word "pointer" was introduced only in later tasks; "address variable" was used first). Respect it — never introduce a term the user is saving for later. ### 2. Pick the task number and base name - Next number = highest existing `docs/taskN/` + 1. - `` is snake_case and shared by all files (e.g. `bitwise_operators`, `address_variables`). Worksheet file is `_worksheet.md`. ### 3. Propose an outline — THIS IS THE REVIEW GATE Do **not** create any files yet. Present a written outline and ask the user to review and discuss it. Include: - **Task number, title, and base filename.** - **Worksheet**: the "golden rule" blockquote idea; the ordered list of iterations, each as a one-line idea plus what the student *sets up* and *observes*; any C programs to be written; the practice set; the reference-table topics; and a note that a Telugu "New Words" table will close it. If the topic suits discovery-first teaching, offer that structure (observe sample(s) → student forms a theory → then the explanation) as an option. - **Questions**: the parts (e.g. A = MCQ, B = fill-in-the-blanks, C = scenarios / trace) and rough counts, plus the kinds of items. Note that questions reveal no answers and that **titles must not give away what to observe**. - **Answers**: mirrors the question numbering, every answer with reasoning, closing "pattern to notice" note. - **What will be verified** (programs compiled, arithmetic/traces checked). Then explicitly invite review: the user may change scope, iterations, examples, counts, terminology, or pedagogy. **Iterate on the outline until the user clearly confirms.** Only a clear go-ahead ("yes", "create it", "confirmed") unlocks step 4. ### 4. On confirmation — create the files Create under `docs/taskN/`: - `_worksheet.md`, `_questions.md`, `_answers.md` following the formats in `CLAUDE.md` (a/b/c iterations + "Takeaway to say out loud"; one-page reference; New Words table; question parts; reasoned answers). - **Verify everything first.** Compile and run every C program and every trace in the scratchpad; check all arithmetic by hand. In sample debugger transcripts use **Linux/WSL-style** addresses (`0x00007fffffff...`, `libc` frames), never the macOS values this machine prints. Do **not** rely on this machine's stack layout for answers — for question snippets that must be portable, use address variables into **arrays** (element layout is guaranteed) so answers match the students' Ubuntu exactly. Keep any deliberate design constraint (e.g. "int only") silent — it shapes the examples but is never announced to students. - Create the three viewers by copying the most recent slim viewer of each kind (e.g. from `docs/task14/`) and changing **only**: ``, `<body class>` (`worksheet`/`questions`/`answers`), `.brand` text, the topbar stage chips, and the status-line text. Everything else comes from `docs/assets/viewer.css` and `docs/assets/viewer.js`. **A viewer's `.html` basename must exactly equal its `.md` basename** (the shared JS derives the markdown filename from the page URL). - **Update `docs/tasks.html`**: add one `<li>` to the `.tasklist` of whichever topic group the task belongs to (`#linux`, `#c`, `#memory`, `#debug`, `#tools`, `#python`), in task-number order within that group — ```html <li><span class="num">Task N</span> <a class="title" href="taskN/<base>_worksheet.html"><Title></a> <a class="q" href="taskN/<base>_questions.html">Questions</a> <a class="q" href="taskN/<base>_answers.html">ans</a></li> ``` (For a tool/reference task with no question bank, replace the two `.q` links with `<span class="only">worksheet only</span>` or `<span class="only">reference</span>`. Use `Extra Questions`/`extra ans` for an `_extra_` bank.) - **Update `docs/index.html`**: add the number to that group's path chip (e.g. `tasks 3, 5, 7`), bump the worksheet count in `.facts`, and — if the batch is moving on to this task — update the `WHERE WE ARE NOW` block. Both spots are marked with comments in the file. ### 5. Verify and report - Serve `docs/` (`python3 -m http.server`) and confirm every new page and its markdown return 200; confirm each viewer's derived markdown exists. - Report what was created: the files, the worksheet's iterations, the question counts, and confirmation that programs/answers were verified. ## Guardrails - **Never create files before the user confirms the outline** (step 3). - One new idea per iteration; predict-before-reveal; the New Words Telugu table is always the last worksheet section. - Don't announce design constraints to students; don't introduce staged vocabulary early. - Verify by running, not by assuming; keep transcripts Ubuntu/WSL-accurate. - Match the file/viewer conventions exactly so the shared assets keep working. For the standard you are defining for students, I would separate **linting** from **type checking**: * **Ruff** → coding style, common errors, imports, unused variables, etc. * **Pyright** → type correctness and enforcement of your type-hint discipline. Ruff supports project configuration through `pyproject.toml` or `ruff.toml`. ([Astral Docs][1]) ### 1. Project structure For a student project: ```text my-project/ ├── pyproject.toml ├── main.py └── student.py ``` Put the rules in `pyproject.toml`. For example: ```toml [tool.ruff] line-length = 88 [tool.ruff.lint] select = [ "E", # pycodestyle "F", # Pyflakes "I", # import sorting "B", # bugbear ] ``` Then simply run: ```bash ruff check . ``` Ruff automatically looks for the configuration file in the project hierarchy. ([Astral Docs][1]) You can also check one file: ```bash ruff check main.py ``` And automatically fix supported problems: ```bash ruff check . --fix ``` ### 2. Type checking is separate For your particular rule: ```python age: int = 20 age = "twenty" ``` you want a **type checker**, not just a conventional linter. For example, with Pyright: ```bash pyright . ``` So your student workflow becomes: ```text Python Program │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ Ruff Pyright │ │ Code quality Type correctness Common errors Type consistency Imports Function contracts Style Data structures │ │ └────────┬────────┘ ↓ Good Python ``` ### 3. The important part for your teaching model You can make `pyproject.toml` the **coding contract for the entire class/project**. For example: ```toml [tool.ruff] line-length = 88 [tool.ruff.lint] select = ["E", "F", "I", "B"] ``` And then a Pyright configuration can define the type-checking strictness. Students don't need to remember dozens of commands. They just run: ```bash ruff check . pyright . ``` or eventually one project command that runs both. ### 4. IDE integration In VS Code, Ruff can provide diagnostics while students are editing, and it can use the project's `pyproject.toml`/`ruff.toml` configuration. ([Astral Docs][2]) That means students can get: ```text student.py age: int = 20 age = "twenty" ^^^^^^^^^ Type error ``` **while writing the code**, rather than discovering it later. --- ### One important distinction I would teach your students these three terms separately: | Tool | Question it answers | | ---------------- | -------------------------------------- | | **Formatter** | "How should my code look?" | | **Linter** | "Is my code written properly?" | | **Type checker** | "Are my types consistent and correct?" | For your **AI-native Python coding standard**, I'd make all three part of the development workflow: ```text AI generates code ↓ Formatter ↓ Ruff ↓ Pyright ↓ Tests ↓ Commit ``` That is a very strong workflow for the students you are training because the **type annotations become both a human-readable specification and a machine-checkable constraint for AI-generated code**. # Why We Should Follow Type Hints in Python

## Core Principle

Going forward, our Python coding standard is:

> **Every variable should have a clearly intended type, and that type
> should not change during the variable's lifetime.**

``` python
name: str = "Ravi"
age: int = 20
marks: list[int] = [80, 90, 85]
```

Avoid reusing a variable for another type:

``` python
age: int = 20
age = "twenty"   # Don't do this
```

Python is still dynamically typed; this is a **coding discipline**, not
a claim that Python is statically typed.

## Why This Matters

### 1. Makes intent explicit

``` python
age: int = 20
```

The type of the data is immediately visible to students, developers, and
tools.

### 2. Makes data structures easier to understand

``` python
student: dict[str, str] = {
    "name": "Ravi",
    "city": "Vizag"
}
```

Students immediately learn:

``` text
dict[key_type, value_type]

dict[str, str]
     ↑    ↑
   key   value
```

Similarly:

``` python
marks: dict[str, int]
numbers: list[int]
names: list[str]
```

This makes the **shape of data** explicit.

### 3. Makes function contracts clear

``` python
def calculate_average(marks: list[int]) -> float:
    ...
```

Students can immediately see:

``` text
Input  → list[int]
Output → float
```

### 4. Helps tools catch mistakes

Type checkers such as Pyright and mypy can detect inconsistent
assignments and incorrect function arguments before runtime.

### 5. Improves AI code generation

This is especially important for AI-native development.

Compare:

``` python
data = get_student()
```

with:

``` python
data: dict[str, int] = get_student()
```

The second gives an AI coding tool much stronger information about the
programmer's intent.

Type hints therefore act as **constraints on AI-generated code**:

``` text
Less information
      ↓
more possible interpretations
      ↓
more opportunities for incorrect code

More type information
      ↓
fewer possible interpretations
      ↓
more precise code
```

### 6. Creates a foundation for modern Python

Type hints naturally lead students from:

``` text
Variables
   ↓
list[T] and dict[K, V]
   ↓
Functions with typed interfaces
   ↓
Classes / dataclasses
   ↓
JSON / APIs
   ↓
Backend applications
   ↓
AI applications
```

## Our Python Coding Standard

1.  **Use type hints for variables.**
2.  **Keep a variable's intended type stable.**
3.  **Specify function parameter and return types.**
4.  **Specify element types for lists and key/value types for
    dictionaries.**
5.  **Use a type checker in larger projects.**

## The Bigger Picture

Type hints benefit **three participants** in modern software
development:

``` text
                         Explicit Types
                              │
               ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
               ↓              ↓              ↓
            Student        Developer      AI Tools
               │              │              │
               ↓              ↓              ↓
          Understand       Understand      Generate
           data better      code better    better code
```

-   **Students** → clarity and programming discipline
-   **Developers** → contracts, readability, and maintainability
-   **AI tools** → stronger context and constraints for code generation

> **Write code that clearly communicates the shape, type, and intent of
> data --- to humans and to AI coding tools.**

# Pull Requests — What Is Actually Happening

**This page is different from the other tasks.** There is nothing to set up and nothing to run. You already know how to open a pull request, leave a review and merge it — you have done it. This page explains **what Git and the website are doing while you click**, so that when something behaves strangely you know why.

Read it once from top to bottom. After that, keep it as a reference: the one-page summary at the end has the tables you will actually come back for.

**Assumed:** Task 21 (Git Internals). Everything here leans on three facts from that task — a commit is an object named by a hash of its contents, a branch is a small text file holding one such hash, and a "protected branch" is a `pre-receive` hook on the server saying no.

**Commands in this page are illustrations, not instructions.** They are shown with their real output to make a point. You are not expected to run them, though nothing stops you.

> **The golden rule of pull requests**
> A pull request is **not a Git command.** Type `git pull-request` and Git will tell you no such thing exists. A PR is a *record kept by a website*, saying: "branch X would like to go into branch Y." The commits are already on the server **before** the PR exists. Underneath every PR — however long the discussion, however many reviewers — there is only ever **two branch names and one merge.**

*(A note on the examples: two people share one repository. **Asha** writes a change; **Ravi** reviews it. The commit hashes shown are from a real run — yours would be different, for the reason Task 21 gave: a commit contains its author and its timestamp.)*

---

## 1. A pull request is not a Git thing

Git does not have pull requests. Not in any version, not with any flag:

```
$ git pull-request
git: 'pull-request' is not a git command. See 'git --help'.
```

The whole idea belongs to the **forge** — the website hosting your repository: GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket. Git provides commits, branches and merging. The forge adds a place to *talk about a merge before it happens*.

So what exists on the server when a PR is open? Exactly this — and nothing more:

```
$ git ls-remote origin
11a9d5f5d2ed6f35624137bbfdc8eedc3d50e155	HEAD
b17cc20f028d01533aab78433ea5e787c2f70fb5	refs/heads/feature/greet
11a9d5f5d2ed6f35624137bbfdc8eedc3d50e155	refs/heads/main
```

Two branches. That is the entire Git-side content of the pull request. Asha's commits arrived on the server when she ran `git push`; the PR did not carry them there. Opening the PR:

- creates **no** new object in `.git/objects/`,
- moves **no** branch,
- changes **nothing** in the repository at all.

It writes a row in GitHub's own database: *PR #7, base `main`, compare `feature/greet`, state open, author Asha.* That is why opening and closing a PR is instant, and why you can close one and open it again with no effect on your code.

This also explains a thing that confuses people: **the PR is not a copy of your work.** If someone deletes the `feature/greet` branch from the server, the pull request has nothing left to show.

**Say it out loud:** "The push moves the commits. The pull request is just a note asking someone to merge them."

---
===== one-page ref =====
## One-page reference

**Anatomy of a pull request**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| base | the branch the work should end up in (`main`) |
| compare / head | the branch holding the work (`feature/greet`) |
| merge base | newest commit both branches share — `git merge-base A B` |
| the diff | merge base ↔ tip of compare (a **three-dot** diff) |
| draft | open, but explicitly not ready to merge |
| the PR itself | a row in the forge's database; **no** Git object |

**Two dots vs three dots**

| Form | Compares | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `main..feature` | tip ↔ tip | how the two branches differ |
| `main...feature` | **merge base** ↔ tip of feature | what feature adds — **this is the PR's Files changed** |

**The three merge buttons**

| | Parents | Original commits | History |
|---|---|---|---|
| Merge commit | **two** | kept, same hashes | shows the branch |
| Squash and merge | one | replaced by one new commit | straight line, one commit per PR |
| Rebase and merge | one | replayed, **new hashes** | straight line, commits kept |

All three produce the **same tree** — identical files. Only the history differs.

**Why the button is grey**

- conflicts with base *(the only Git-level reason)*
- a required check is failing — or still pending
- not enough approvals
- someone's "Request changes" is unresolved
- unresolved conversations
- CODEOWNERS has not approved
- branch is behind base *(if that rule is on)*
- you lack permission to merge

**Review actions that move the gate:** Approve, Request changes. Nothing else.

**PR end states**

| State | Commits on base? | Reopenable |
|---|---|---|
| Merged | yes | no |
| Closed | no | yes, while the branch exists |

# Linters, Formatters and Type Checkers — Letting a Machine Read Your Code First

**This page is reading material, not a worksheet.** There are no iterations and no practice section. It explains the three tools that read your Python code *before you run it*, and how one small file — `pyproject.toml` — turns our coding standard into something a machine checks instead of something you have to remember.

**Assumed:** Task 32 (Why We Should Follow Type Hints in Python). That task gave us a rule: *every variable has a clearly intended type, and that type does not change*. Task 32 asked you to follow it. This task hands the rule to a machine.

**The commands here are real.** Every piece of output on this page came from an actual run — `ruff` 0.16.3 and `pyright` 1.1.411. You are welcome to type them yourself on your VM; nothing here will damage anything.

> **The golden rule of this page**
> Three tools, three different questions — and they are **not** interchangeable.
> A **formatter** answers *"how should my code look?"*
> A **linter** answers *"is my code written properly?"*
> A **type checker** answers *"are my types consistent?"*
> A linter will read `age: int = 20` followed by `age = "twenty"` and say **"All checks passed!"** — because that is not its question.

---

## 1. Three questions, three tools

Beginners meet all of these as "the thing that shows red squiggles in the editor" and assume they are one tool. They are not. Each one refuses to answer the others' question.

| Tool | The question it answers | Example of what it catches |
|---|---|---|
| **Formatter** (`ruff format`) | How should my code *look*? | inconsistent spacing, a line that runs off the screen |
| **Linter** (`ruff check`) | Is my code *written properly*? | an import you never used, a variable you assigned and forgot |
| **Type checker** (`pyright`) | Are my types *consistent*? | `age: int = 20` then `age = "twenty"` |

Two of these are the same program. **Ruff** is both the formatter and the linter — `ruff format` and `ruff check` are two different commands of one tool. **Pyright** is a separate program entirely, and it is the only one of the three that understands what `list[int]` *means*.

Drawn as one picture:

```text
                 Python Program
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              ↓                 ↓
            Ruff             Pyright
              │                 │
        Code quality        Type correctness
        Common errors       Type consistency
        Imports             Function contracts
        Style               Data structures
              │                 │
              └────────┬────────┘
                       ↓
                  Good Python
```

**Say it out loud:** "Ruff asks how it is written. Pyright asks whether the types agree. Neither one answers the other's question."

---

## 2. Installing them on your VM

Both tools are ordinary programs you install once. Inside your project's virtual environment:

```
$ pip install ruff pyright
```

Then check that they are really there. This is the output from the versions used throughout this page:

```
$ ruff --version
ruff 0.16.3

$ pyright --version
pyright 1.1.411
```

A note about Pyright: it is written in TypeScript, so the first time you run it, it quietly downloads a small copy of Node.js for itself. That first run is slow. Every run after it is fast. Nothing is wrong.

**Say it out loud:** "Two installs, two `--version` checks. If both print a version, I am ready."

---

## 3. `pyproject.toml` — the coding contract

Here is the project we will use for the rest of this page:

```text
my-project/
├── pyproject.toml
├── main.py
└── student.py
```

The rules live in **`pyproject.toml`** at the top of the project:

```toml
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 88

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = [
    "E",      # pycodestyle
    "F",      # Pyflakes
    "I",      # import sorting
    "B",      # bugbear
]
```

Those single letters each switch on a whole family of rules:

| Letter | Family | What it watches for |
|---|---|---|
| `E` | pycodestyle | layout: line too long, spacing around operators |
| `F` | Pyflakes | real mistakes: unused imports, unused variables, undefined names |
| `I` | isort | imports in a sensible, sorted order |
| `B` | flake8-bugbear | traps that are legal Python but almost always a bug |

This file is the important idea of the whole task. It is **checked into the repository**, so it is not *your* settings — it is **the project's** settings. Everyone who clones the repo gets the same rules, and the editor, the terminal and (later) the server all read this one file. Nobody argues about line length in a review, because the file already decided.

Ruff finds it by itself. You never pass it on the command line: run `ruff` anywhere inside the project and it walks up the folders until it finds `pyproject.toml`.

**Say it out loud:** "`pyproject.toml` is the coding contract for the whole project, not a setting on my laptop."

## 4. Ruff, on a file with real problems

Here is `student.py`. It runs. Python has no complaint about it at all:

```python
import sys
import json
import os


def add_student(name: str, marks: list[int] = []) -> dict[str, object]:
    total = 0
    for m in marks:
        total = total + m
    average = total / len(marks)
    label = "pass"
    return {"name": name, "marks": marks, "average": average}


def report(students: list[dict[str, object]]) -> None:
    for s in students:
        print(json.dumps(s))
        print("Student " + str(s["name"]) + " has an average of " + str(s["average"]) + " marks out of a hundred")
```

Now let the linter read it:

```
$ ruff check .
I001 [*] Import block is un-sorted or un-formatted
 --> student.py:1:1
  |
1 | / import sys
2 | | import json
3 | | import os
  | |_________^
help: Organize imports

F401 [*] `sys` imported but unused
 --> student.py:1:8
  |
1 | import sys
  |        ^^^
help: Remove unused import: `sys`

F401 [*] `os` imported but unused
 --> student.py:3:8
  |
3 | import os
  |        ^^
help: Remove unused import: `os`

B006 Do not use mutable data structures for argument defaults
 --> student.py:6:47
  |
6 | def add_student(name: str, marks: list[int] = []) -> dict[str, object]:
  |                                               ^^
help: Replace with `None`; initialize within function

F841 Local variable `label` is assigned to but never used
  --> student.py:11:5
   |
11 |     label = "pass"
   |     ^^^^^
help: Remove assignment to unused variable `label`

E501 Line too long (114 > 88)
  --> student.py:18:89

Found 6 errors.
[*] 3 fixable with the `--fix` option (2 hidden fixes can be enabled with the `--unsafe-fixes` option).
```

Six findings in a file Python was perfectly happy to run. Read them one at a time:

- **`I001` — imports not sorted.** `sys`, `json`, `os` is not alphabetical. Trivial, but a machine can keep it perfect forever, so why should a human think about it.
- **`F401` — imported but unused.** Twice. We imported `sys` and `os` and never used either. Harmless today; misleading to the next reader, who assumes the file touches the operating system.
- **`B006` — mutable default argument.** This is the serious one. `marks: list[int] = []` creates **one** list when the function is *defined*, not a fresh one per call — so every caller who leaves `marks` out shares the same list. This is legal Python, it runs, and it is almost never what anyone meant.
- **`F841` — assigned but never used.** `label = "pass"` was computed and thrown away. Usually the sign of an unfinished thought: someone meant to put it in the returned dictionary.
- **`E501` — line too long.** 114 characters where the contract said 88.

Notice the shape of every message: **rule code**, then `file:line:column`, then the offending line with a `^^^` pointing at exactly the spot, then a `help:` line saying what to do. That shape never changes, so once you can read one message you can read all of them.

**Say it out loud:** "Every finding is a rule code, a place, and a suggestion. The file ran fine — that was never the question."

## 5. What the machine may fix, and what it refuses to guess

Look again at the last line of that report: `3 fixable with the --fix option`. Ruff is telling you which of the six it is willing to repair by itself. Ask it to:

```
$ ruff check . --fix
B006 Do not use mutable data structures for argument defaults
 --> student.py:4:47
F841 Local variable `label` is assigned to but never used
  --> student.py:9:5
E501 Line too long (114 > 88)
  --> student.py:16:89

Found 5 errors (2 fixed, 3 remaining).
```

The two unused imports are gone from the file. And so is `I001` — once `sys` and `os` were deleted, only `import json` was left, and a single import is trivially sorted. One fix removed two findings.

Now the formatter takes its turn:

```
$ ruff format .
1 file reformatted, 1 file left unchanged
```

It rewrote the over-long `print` into something that fits:

```python
        print(
            "Student "
            + str(s["name"])
            + " has an average of "
            + str(s["average"])
            + " marks out of a hundred"
        )
```

`E501` is now gone too. Check once more:

```
$ ruff check .
B006 Do not use mutable data structures for argument defaults
F841 Local variable `label` is assigned to but never used

Found 2 errors.
```

Two left — and these two are left **on purpose**. Look at what fixing them would require:

- For `B006`, the machine would have to change the function's behaviour. Should the default be `None` and a new list made inside? Should the parameter be required instead? Those are different programs, and only you know which one you meant.
- For `F841`, deleting `label = "pass"` is one answer. Putting it into the returned dictionary is another — and more likely what the author intended. Deleting a line is not a safe guess when the line was probably meant to be *used*.

This is the boundary worth memorising: **a tool may rewrite what cannot change the meaning of your program.** Anything past that line, it points at and stops. (That is also what "unsafe fixes" means — repairs Ruff *can* make but which might change behaviour, so it will not make them unless you insist.)

Fixed by hand, `add_student` becomes:

```python
def add_student(name: str, marks: list[int] | None = None) -> dict[str, object]:
    if marks is None:
        marks = []
    total = 0
    for m in marks:
        total = total + m
    average = total / len(marks)
    return {"name": name, "marks": marks, "average": average}
```

And now:

```
$ ruff check .
All checks passed!
```

**Say it out loud:** "The machine fixes what cannot change the meaning. The rest it points at, because only I know what I meant."

## 6. The one thing Ruff will never tell you

Here is `main.py` — the exact thing Task 32 told us never to do:

```python
age: int = 20
age = "twenty"
print(age)
```

Ask the linter about it:

```
$ ruff check main.py
All checks passed!
```

**All checks passed.** Sit with that for a moment. The file breaks our single most important coding rule, and the linter approves it — not because Ruff is weak, but because this is not Ruff's question. Nothing here is badly *written*: no unused import, no long line, nothing out of order. The mistake is in the **types**, and a linter does not track types.

The same blindness in a more expensive form:

```python
def average(marks: list[int]) -> float:
    return sum(marks) / len(marks)


scores: list[int] = [80, 90, 85]
print(average(scores))

print(average(85))

result: int = average(scores)
```

```
$ ruff check .
All checks passed!
```

Two of those lines are wrong. `average(85)` passes a number where the function's contract clearly says `list[int]`, and it will crash when it runs. `result: int = average(scores)` stores a `float` in something declared `int`. Ruff sees no problem, and it is right not to — that is somebody else's job.

**Say it out loud:** "'All checks passed' means the linter's checks passed. It says nothing about my types."

## 7. Pyright answers the type question

Same files. Different tool:

```
$ pyright .
/home/student/my-project/main.py
  /home/student/my-project/main.py:2:7 - error: Type "Literal['twenty']" is not assignable to declared type "int"
    "Literal['twenty']" is not assignable to "int" (reportAssignmentType)
1 error, 0 warnings, 0 informations
```

There it is. Line 2, column 7 — the string. `Literal['twenty']` is Pyright being precise: it knows not just that this is a `str`, but *which* `str`. And `is not assignable to declared type "int"` is Pyright quoting **your own annotation** back at you. You declared `int`; you assigned a string; that is the whole complaint.

Now the `average` file:

```
$ pyright .
/home/student/my-project/marks.py
  /home/student/my-project/marks.py:8:15 - error: Argument of type "Literal[85]" cannot be assigned to parameter "marks" of type "list[int]" in function "average"
    "Literal[85]" is not assignable to "list[int]" (reportArgumentType)
  /home/student/my-project/marks.py:10:15 - error: Type "float" is not assignable to declared type "int"
    "float" is not assignable to "int" (reportAssignmentType)
2 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations
```

Both mistakes, caught before the program ran once. And notice **how** they were caught: Pyright never executed `average`. It read the line `def average(marks: list[int]) -> float:` and treated it as a promise. The type hints you wrote in Task 32 are what made this possible — with them removed, Pyright would have nothing to check against and would fall silent, exactly like Ruff.

That is the sentence to carry out of this task: **a type hint is not a comment. It is a claim, and Pyright is the thing that tests the claim.**

**Say it out loud:** "The annotation is the promise. Pyright checks that the rest of the code keeps it."

## 9. `basic` and `strict`

Pyright's strictness is a setting, and it lives in the same contract file:

```toml
[tool.pyright]
typeCheckingMode = "basic"
```

Consider a file with no annotations at all:

```python
def shout(word):
    return word.upper()
```

In `basic`, Pyright says nothing about it. It cannot know what `word` is, so it declines to guess and moves on. Switch one word in `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
typeCheckingMode = "strict"
```

```
$ pyright .
/home/student/my-project/helper.py
  helper.py:1:5 - error: Return type is unknown (reportUnknownParameterType)
  helper.py:1:11 - error: Type of parameter "word" is unknown (reportUnknownParameterType)
  helper.py:1:11 - error: Type annotation is missing for parameter "word" (reportMissingParameterType)
  helper.py:2:12 - error: Type of "upper" is unknown (reportUnknownMemberType)
  helper.py:2:12 - error: Return type is unknown (reportUnknownVariableType)
```

Five complaints about a two-line function. In `strict`, "I don't know what this is" is itself an error. Same code, same tool — a different answer, because you changed what counts as acceptable.

For your own projects, start on `basic` and move to `strict` when the code is fully annotated. `strict` on an old unannotated project produces hundreds of errors and teaches nothing. `strict` on code written the Task 32 way produces almost none — which is rather the point.

**Say it out loud:** "Strictness is a choice written in the file, not a property of the tool."

## 10. Where each tool sits in the workflow

Put the pieces in the order you actually use them:

```text
AI generates code
       ↓
   ruff format      ← make it look right
       ↓
   ruff check       ← is it written properly?
       ↓
    pyright         ← do the types agree?
       ↓
     tests          ← does it do the right thing?
       ↓
    commit
```

The order is not decoration. Formatting first means the linter is not distracted by layout. The linter next, because an unused import is cheaper to find than a type error. Pyright after that. Only then tests, which are the slowest and the most valuable.

And they really are ordered by *what they can know*. Take our corrected `add_student` — it passes everything:

```
$ ruff check .
All checks passed!
$ pyright .
0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations
```

Then you call it with no marks at all:

```
>>> add_student("Ravi")
  File "/home/student/my-project/student.py", line 10, in add_student
    average = total / len(marks)
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
```

Clean on both tools, and it still crashed. Neither tool ever claimed otherwise: an empty list is a perfectly valid `list[int]`, so there was nothing for Pyright to object to. **Dividing by its length is a mistake about meaning, not about types** — and mistakes about meaning are what tests are for. That is exactly why `tests` sits below `pyright` in the diagram and not above it.

This chain matters more, not less, when the code came from an AI. You cannot read every generated line as carefully as one you typed yourself — but the format, lint and type steps read all of it, every time, at the same standard. Your type hints become the specification the generated code is measured against.

**Say it out loud:** "Format, lint, type-check, test — cheapest question first, and each one only answers its own."

| Keep a variable's intended type stable | Pyright — `reportAssignmentType` |

## One-page reference

**The three questions**

| Tool | Command | Question |
|---|---|---|
| Formatter | `ruff format .` | How should my code look? |
| Linter | `ruff check .` | Is my code written properly? |
| Type checker | `pyright .` | Are my types consistent? |

**Everyday commands**

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ruff check .` | lint the whole project |
| `ruff check main.py` | lint one file |
| `ruff check . --fix` | lint and repair what is safe to repair |
| `ruff format .` | reformat every file |
| `ruff format --check .` | say what *would* change; change nothing |
| `pyright .` | type-check the whole project |
| `pyright main.py` | type-check one file |

Exit code `0` = clean, non-zero = findings. Both tools search upward for `pyproject.toml`, so run them from anywhere inside the project.

**The rule families we switch on**

| Letter | Family | Watches for |
|---|---|---|
| `E` | pycodestyle | line length, spacing |
| `F` | Pyflakes | unused imports, unused variables, undefined names |
| `I` | isort | import order |
| `B` | bugbear | legal code that is almost certainly a bug |

**Rule codes seen in this task**

| Code | Meaning | Auto-fixable |
|---|---|---|
| `I001` | import block un-sorted | yes |
| `F401` | imported but unused | yes |
| `F841` | assigned but never used | no — you may have meant to use it |
| `E501` | line too long | by the **formatter**, not by `--fix` |
| `B006` | mutable default argument | no — the repair changes behaviour |
| `reportAssignmentType` | value does not match the declared type | Pyright |
| `reportArgumentType` | argument does not match the parameter type | Pyright |

**The contract file**

```toml
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 88

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "B"]

[tool.pyright]
typeCheckingMode = "basic"    # "strict" once the code is fully annotated
```

**The workflow**

```text
format  →  lint  →  type-check  →  test  →  commit
```

**Three sentences worth remembering**

- A linter that says *All checks passed!* has said nothing about your types.
- A tool fixes only what cannot change the meaning of your program.
- Code that passes both tools can still be wrong — that is what tests are for.

# Linters, Formatters and Type Checkers — Answer Key

**Check the reasoning, not just the letter.** Every tool message printed below is real output from `ruff` 0.16.3 and `pyright` 1.1.411 on exactly the code in the question. If your letter was right but your reason was different, the reason is the part to fix.

---

## Part A — Multiple Choice

**A1 — B. How should my code look?**

`ruff format` only rearranges appearance: indentation, spacing, where a long expression is broken across lines. It never changes what the program does. "Is my code written properly?" is `ruff check` (A), and "are my types consistent?" is `pyright` (C). D is the question tests answer — no tool on this page can tell you whether your program computes the right answer.

**A2 — C. `All checks passed!`**

This is the most important item in Part A. The file breaks our Task 32 rule in the plainest possible way, and the linter approves it:

```
$ ruff check .
All checks passed!
```

Nothing here is badly *written* — no unused import, no long line, nothing out of order. The mistake is entirely in the **types**, and Ruff does not track types. D is the real message for this code, but Pyright prints it, not Ruff. A is nonsense (`age` is a variable, not an import).

**A3 — A. `F401`, an imported module that is never used**

Deleting an import nobody uses cannot change what the program does, so Ruff will do it for you. The others are all refusals, for the same underlying reason in different clothes:

- **B006** — repairing it means changing the function's behaviour. Default to `None` and build the list inside? Make the parameter required? Different programs. Only you know which.
- **F841** — deleting `label = "pass"` is one answer; *using* the value is the more likely one. Deleting a line that was probably meant to be used is not a safe guess.
- **E501** — a long line does get fixed, but by `ruff format`, not by `--fix`. The two commands have different jobs.

**A4 — C. in `pyproject.toml`, committed to the repository**

That is what makes the rules the **project's** and not yours. Everyone who clones gets them, and the editor and the terminal read the same file, so they cannot disagree. A gives every student different rules. B means the rules are whatever each person remembers to type. D is not a thing any tool reads.

**A5 — B. layout — line length and spacing**

`E` is pycodestyle. The others in our `select` list: `F` is Pyflakes (A — unused imports, unused variables), `I` is import sorting (C), `B` is bugbear (D — legal code that is almost certainly a bug).

**A6 — A. `0`**

The ordinary Unix convention you already know: `0` means nothing to report, non-zero means findings.

```
$ ruff check c3.py ; echo $?
All checks passed!
0
$ ruff check c1.py > /dev/null ; echo $?
1
```

This is exactly why these commands can sit inside a script or a check that runs on every pull request — the script needs a yes/no, and the exit code is it.

**A7 — C. `basic` reports none, `strict` reports several**

In `basic`, Pyright cannot tell what `word` is, so it declines to guess and stays quiet. Switch one word in `pyproject.toml` and "I don't know what this is" becomes an error in itself:

```
$ pyright .
  helper.py:1:5 - error: Return type is unknown (reportUnknownParameterType)
  helper.py:1:11 - error: Type of parameter "word" is unknown (reportUnknownParameterType)
  helper.py:1:11 - error: Type annotation is missing for parameter "word" (reportMissingParameterType)
  helper.py:2:12 - error: Type of "upper" is unknown (reportUnknownMemberType)
  helper.py:2:12 - error: Return type is unknown (reportUnknownVariableType)
```

Five complaints about a two-line function. Same code, same tool — strictness is a choice written in the file. D is true as far as it goes (the code *is* valid Python) but that was never the question either tool was asking.

**A8 — C. `pyright`**

Two giveaways, and you should be able to use either one. The **rule name in brackets**: Ruff's codes are a letter and digits (`F401`, `E501`, `B006`); Pyright's are words beginning with `report…`. And the **shape**: Pyright leads with `file:line:col - error:`, Ruff leads with the rule code and puts the location on an arrow line beneath. D is wrong because nothing ran — that is the whole point of a type checker.

---

## Part B — Fill in the Blanks

**B1 — `--fix`** → `ruff check . --fix`. Remember what it will not touch, from A3.

**B2 — `pyright`** → `pyright .` The `.` means "this folder and everything under it", the same as in `ruff check .`

**B3 — `F401`** — *imported but unused*. An `F` code, so it comes from Pyflakes: a real mistake, not a matter of style.

**B4 — `E501`** — *line too long*. An `E` code: pycodestyle, layout.

**B5 — `pyproject.toml`** — and it must be committed. Both tools search **upward** through the folders until they find it, which is why you can run them from anywhere inside the project without passing the file.

**B6 — `--check`** → `ruff format --check .` It reports what would change and changes nothing. Useful when you want to *ask* rather than *act* — for instance in a check that must not modify anyone's files.

**B7 — `0`** — see A6.

---

## Part C — Read the Program

A quick way to check your work before reading each one: the deciding question is always *which* question is being broken. If the code is written untidily, it is Ruff. If the code is written neatly but the types disagree, it is Pyright.

### C1 — Ruff · `F401` · delete `import math`

```
$ ruff check c1.py
F401 [*] `math` imported but unused
 --> c1.py:1:8
  |
1 | import math
  |        ^^^^
help: Remove unused import: `math`

Found 1 error.
[*] 1 fixable with the `--fix` option.
```

`random` is used on the last line; `math` is never used at all. Pyright says `0 errors` — every type here is fine. Note the `[*]`: this is one Ruff *will* fix for you, because removing a dead import cannot change what the program does.

**Not `I001`** — `math`, `random` is already alphabetical.

### C2 — Ruff · `B006` · take the list out of the default

```
$ ruff check c2.py
B006 Do not use mutable data structures for argument defaults
 --> c2.py:1:41
  |
1 | def add_tag(tag: str, tags: list[str] = []) -> list[str]:
  |                                         ^^
help: Replace with `None`; initialize within function

Found 1 error.
No fixes available (1 hidden fix can be enabled with the `--unsafe-fixes` option).
```

This is the one worth slowing down for, because the code looks completely reasonable and Python raises no objection. The `[]` is created **once, when the function is defined** — not fresh on each call. So every caller who leaves `tags` out is handed the *same* list:

```
>>> add_tag("python")
['python']
>>> add_tag("linux")
['python', 'linux']
>>> add_tag("git")
['python', 'linux', 'git']
```

Three separate calls, and the tags pile up. Almost nobody means this. The repair:

```python
def add_tag(tag: str, tags: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
    if tags is None:
        tags = []
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags
```

`None` is not mutable, so there is nothing to share, and a new list is built on each call that needs one. Notice Ruff would not make this change for you — it alters behaviour, and altering behaviour is your decision.

### C3 — Neither · no rule code · change nothing

```
$ ruff check c3.py
All checks passed!
$ pyright c3.py
0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations
```

Both tools clean. `count` is declared `int` and only ever holds `int`; `total` likewise. Nothing unused, nothing too long, nothing out of order. This is what code that follows the Task 32 standard looks like to the machines.

If you wrote a rule code here, look again at what each tool actually asks — there is no rule against a variable being reassigned. `count = count + 1` is perfectly fine; **`count = "one"` would not be.** The rule is about the *type* staying stable, not the value.

### C4 — Pyright · `reportAssignmentType` · keep `price` a number

```

All checks passed!

$ pyright c4.py
c4.py:2:9 - error: Type "Literal['ninety nine']" is not assignable to declared type "float"

1 error, 0 warnings, 0 informations
```

Exactly the A2 situation with different names. Ruff has no complaint — nothing is written untidily. Pyright quotes your own annotation back at you: you declared `float` on line 1, you assigned a string on line 2.

`Literal['ninety nine']` is Pyright being precise. It knows not just that this is a `str`, but *which* `str` — the exact value it can see in the source.

The fix depends on what you meant: if the price really is 99.5, delete line 2; if it is text you need to display, that belongs in a *different* variable with its own name and its own type.

### C5 — Pyright · `reportArgumentType` · pass a string to `greet`

```
$ ruff check c5.py
All checks passed!

$ pyright c5.py
c5.py:5:13 - error: Argument of type "Literal[42]" cannot be assigned to parameter "name" of type "str" in function "greet"
  "Literal[42]" is not assignable to "str" (reportArgumentType)
1 error, 0 warnings, 0 informations
```

`greet` promises to accept a `str`. Line 5 hands it `42`. This one is worth noticing for a second reason: it would have **crashed when it ran** — `"Hello, " + 42` raises `TypeError`. Pyright found it without running the program at all.

How? It never executed `greet`. It read the line `def greet(name: str) -> str:` and treated your annotation as a promise, then checked the call against it. This is the whole return on the type-hint discipline from Task 32: **an annotation is not a comment, it is a claim, and Pyright is the thing that tests the claim.** Strip the `: str` off and Pyright falls silent — with nothing promised, there is nothing to break.

Fix: `print(greet("Ravi"))` — or `print(greet(str(42)))` if a number really is what you have.

### C6 — Ruff · `F841` · use `text`, or drop it

```
$ ruff check c6.py
F841 Local variable `text` is assigned to but never used
 --> c6.py:5:5
  |
4 | def save(data: dict[str, int]) -> None:
5 |     text = json.dumps(data)
  |     ^^^^
help: Remove assignment to unused variable `text`

Found 1 error.
No fixes available (1 hidden fix can be enabled with the `--unsafe-fixes` option).
```

`json.dumps(data)` builds a string and hands it to `text`, and then the function ends. The work is done and thrown away — which is why `F841` is a real-mistake code (`F`) and not a style one. A function called `save` that saves nothing is almost certainly unfinished: someone meant to write it to a file or print it.

**`import json` is *not* flagged here** — it is genuinely used on line 5. That the *result* goes nowhere is a separate complaint, and it gets its own separate code.

And note `No fixes available`: deleting the line would silence the message while making the function even more clearly wrong. Ruff will not do that for you.

### C7 — Both · `F401` and `reportAssignmentType` · delete `import os`, keep `total` an `int`

```
$ ruff check c7.py
F401 [*] `os` imported but unused
 --> c7.py:1:8
  |
1 | import os
  |        ^^
help: Remove unused import: `os`

Found 1 error.

$ pyright c7.py
c7.py:4:9 - error: Type "Literal['one hundred']" is not assignable to declared type "int"
  "Literal['one hundred']" is not assignable to "int" (reportAssignmentType)
1 error, 0 warnings, 0 informations
```

Two problems of two different kinds in five lines, and **each tool sees only its own**. Ruff reports the dead import and says nothing about line 4. Pyright reports line 4 and says nothing about the import — an unused import is not a type error.

If you had run only one of them, you would have fixed half the file and believed you were finished. That is the argument for both commands, not either.

---

## The pattern to notice

Line up what each tool said across all seven programs:

| | Ruff | Pyright |
|---|---|---|
| C1 unused import | `F401` | clean |
| C2 mutable default | `B006` | clean |
| C3 correct code | clean | clean |
| C4 string into a `float` | **clean** | `reportAssignmentType` |
| C5 number into a `str` parameter | **clean** | `reportArgumentType` |
| C6 unused variable | `F841` | clean |
| C7 both kinds at once | `F401` | `reportAssignmentType` |

Look down the two columns. **They almost never light up together** — and where one is silent, the other is not being lenient, it is being asked a different question. Ruff printing `All checks passed!` on C4 and C5 is not Ruff failing; types were never its job.

Three things worth carrying out of this bank:

1. **"All checks passed!" answers one question only.** Never read it as "my code is correct."
2. **A tool repairs only what cannot change the meaning of your program.** Everything past that line it points at and stops — because past that line, the decision is yours.
3. **A type hint is a claim, and Pyright tests it.** Everything Pyright caught here, it caught because someone had written `: float`, `: str`, `: int` first. That is what Task 32 was buying.
